item.title: Diffusion Models, Part 4: Cross-Modal Diffusion and Implementation
item.description:
Diffusion Models, Part 4: Cross-Modal Diffusion and Implementation

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Chapter 7: Cross-Modal Diffusion — Video, 3D, Audio, and Discrete Data

Diffusion models first broke through in image generation, but their core idea — starting from a simple distribution and approaching a complex data distribution through iterative denoising — is not limited to two-dimensional pixels. In recent years, researchers have extended the diffusion framework to a range of modalities, including video, three-dimensional geometry, audio, and discrete symbol sequences, creating the active frontier of cross-modal diffusion. This chapter walks through these directions one by one, focusing on three questions: what is hard about each modality, which part of the diffusion framework the main methods change, and the commonalities and trade-offs among them.

item.description:
Diffusion Models, Part 2: Latent Diffusion and Controllable Generation

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Chapter 3: Conditional Generation and Latent Diffusion Models

3.1 From Unconditional to Conditional Generation

Diffusion models first appeared in the form of unconditional generation: learning a data distribution $p(x)$ and sampling from noise to produce new samples similar to the training data. In practice, however, users need finer control—specifying a class, a text description, a style reference, and so on. Conditional generation aims to learn a conditional distribution $p(x \mid c)$, where $c$ is the conditioning signal, which can be a class label, a text embedding, an image mask, or a spatial structure map.

item.title: Diffusion Models, Part 1: Foundations and Classic Models
item.description:
Diffusion Models, Part 1: Foundations and Classic Models

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Deep Learning Diffusion Models: Foundations and Classic Models

Author: ResearchWriter_基础与经典 Generated: 2026-07-02

Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations and Core Concepts of Diffusion Models

1.1 Introduction and Historical Context

Diffusion models are one of the most important technical paradigms in generative AI today, and their theoretical roots span statistical physics, stochastic processes, and variational inference. In 2015, Sohl-Dickstein et al.1 first drew inspiration from nonequilibrium statistical mechanics and proposed a generative framework that progressively destroys data structure through a forward diffusion process and then restores it through a reverse diffusion process. Then Song & Ermon (2019)2 revisited the problem from the perspective of score matching and proposed the Noise Conditional Score Network (NCSN); Ho et al. (2020)3 developed the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM), which brought diffusion models into practical use through variational inference and a simplified training objective. In 2021, Song et al.4 proposed a unified framework based on stochastic differential equations (SDE), showing that NCSN and DDPM are discretizations of two classes of continuous-time diffusion processes—VE-SDE and VP-SDE—and that both can be described in the same language of “score + SDE.” In 2022, the EDM work by Karras et al.5 systematically elucidated the design space of diffusion models, unifying the choices of preconditioning, loss weighting, and samplers. This chapter starts from the mathematical foundations and systematically builds the core conceptual framework of diffusion models.

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Introduction to Prototype Analysis

In hyperspectral image processing, prototype analysis (Archetypal Analysis, AA) is an unsupervised method for endmember extraction and abundance estimation. Unlike conventional endmember extraction methods, prototype analysis does not assume that endmembers lie at the vertices of a simplex. Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Vertex Component Analysis (VCA) is a fast unsupervised algorithm for extracting endmembers from hyperspectral images. Its main idea is to use the property that endmembers form the vertices of the data cloud in a high-dimensional feature space. By iteratively searching for spectra that lie on the boundary of the data cloud, the algorithm extracts the endmembers. item.title: C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming (Part I)
item.description:
C++ Concurrency and Parallel Programming (Part I)

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Concurrent programs are hard to write not so much because of the sheer number of APIs, but because you must answer three questions clearly: Who owns the data, who may modify it, and what mechanism lets another thread use it safely? This article organizes C++ concurrency and parallel programming around those three questions. The code centers on the C++20 standard library and uses no third-party concurrency library.

This is Part I of the series. It covers, in order, the execution model, the build environment, thread lifecycles and argument passing, shared state and mutexes, multiple locks and deadlock, condition variables, and task result channels such as promise, packaged_task, and async. Part II goes on to discuss atomic variables and memory ordering, C++20’s cancellation and coordination facilities, engineering practice, and the implementation of a complete task processor.

item.title: Maximum Distance (MaxD) Endmember Extraction for Hyperspectral Images
item.description:
Maximum Distance (MaxD) Endmember Extraction for Hyperspectral Images

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

The maximum distance (MaxD) algorithm is an unsupervised endmember extraction method used to identify pure endmember spectra in a hyperspectral image. This post presents the mathematical principle of the MaxD algorithm and a MATLAB implementation.

Algorithm Principle

The MaxD algorithm is based on the following key ideas:

  1. Maximum-distance criterion: Endmember spectra correspond to the sample points that lie farthest apart in feature space. This is because an endmember spectrum represents the spectrum of a pure surface material, whereas a mixed spectrum lies between endmember spectra.

  2. Sequential extraction: The algorithm extracts all endmember spectra one by one, in descending order of the distance between each endmember spectrum and the other spectra.

  3. Vector projection: When a new endmember spectrum is extracted, linear combinations of the known endmember spectra are used to construct a vector space. The new endmember spectrum is the one with the largest projection length in the complementary subspace of that space.

Accurately and promptly detecting changes in land-surface features is essential for environmental monitoring and resource management. Compared with conventional single-band or multispectral remote sensing imagery, hyperspectral imagery contains a large amount of spectral information and therefore performs better at change detection. Subspace learning is an effective tool for analyzing hyperspectral imagery. Its strengths are that it can accurately describe linearly mixed signals and that it offers better signal separability. item.title: A Fast Hyperspectral Image Unmixing Algorithm Based on the Minimum-Volume Simplex
item.description:
A Fast Hyperspectral Image Unmixing Algorithm Based on the Minimum-Volume Simplex

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Hyperspectral remote sensing is a key technique for identifying the endmember constituents within a target region and their proportions. It is widely used in land-cover classification, environmental monitoring, and related fields. Hyperspectral unmixing (HU) is the signal-processing task of analyzing hyperspectral data to identify the endmembers in an image and their corresponding abundances. Craig’s minimum-volume simplex criterion is a classical and effective method for blind unmixing: the vertices of the minimum-volume simplex that encloses the data point cloud are taken as the endmember estimates. Related algorithms are computationally inefficient, however, because they involve complicated volume calculations. HyperCSI (Hyperplane-based Craig-Simplex Identification) does not evaluate a complicated volume function. It uses a geometric theorem instead: an \(N\)-dimensional simplex can be determined by \(N\) hyperplanes (of dimension \(N-2\)). HyperCSI reconstructs Craig’s minimum-volume simplex by constructing \(N\) hyperplanes associated with it. This avoids the volume calculation and is far less expensive than algorithms based on Craig’s criterion.

item.title: The Multi-Head Self-Attention Mechanism in Transformers
item.description:
The Multi-Head Self-Attention Mechanism in Transformers

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

In natural language processing and other sequence-modeling tasks, the Transformer has become a research focus thanks to its strong performance. Multi-head self-attention is one of the Transformer’s core components. What follows looks closely at how it works and how it is implemented.

What Is Self-Attention

The self-attention mechanism lets the model, while encoding a sequence, gather information from the other positions for the representation at each position and update that representation from this information. Unlike recurrent networks such as RNNs and LSTMs, which capture dependence along a sequence step by step, self-attention models dependence between positions directly through attention scores. Modeling long-range dependence directly in this way greatly increases the model’s expressive power.

item.title: Endmember Extraction Using the Pixel Purity Index (PPI) Algorithm
item.description:
Endmember Extraction Using the Pixel Purity Index (PPI) Algorithm

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

The Pixel Purity Index (PPI) algorithm extracts endmember signatures from hyperspectral data cubes. It identifies endmember pixels by projecting dimensionality-reduced data onto randomly generated unit vectors and finding the pixels with the largest projection values.

Algorithm Principle

  1. Perform dimensionality reduction on the hyperspectral data cube, choosing from PCA (Principal Component Analysis), MNF (Maximum Noise Fraction), or no reduction at all.
  2. Generate a set number of random unit vectors (10,000 by default).
  3. Project the reduced data onto each random unit vector and record the maximum projection value obtained by each pixel.
  4. Rank the pixels by their maximum projection values and select the N pixels with the largest values as the endmember signatures.

item.title: Effortless Cross-Device Configuration with Dotfiles and Plugins
item.description:
Effortless Cross-Device Configuration with Dotfiles and Plugins

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Managing dotfiles and configurations for applications like Vim and Tmux across multiple devices can be a daunting task. However, with a few simple steps, you can streamline the process and achieve seamless one-click configuration on any machine.

  1. Version Control: Use Git to track your dotfiles. Create a Git repository and store your configuration files within it. This allows you to manage file versions and sync your setup across different machines.

  2. Symbolic Links: Clone your dotfiles repository on a new machine and create symbolic links pointing to these files. This way, you can maintain the file locations within the repository while the system uses the symbolic links.

  3. Automation Script: Write an installation script that, when you clone the repository on a new machine, automatically creates symbolic links and installs necessary software (like Vim and Tmux plugin managers).

  4. Plugin Managers: For Vim, you can use a plugin manager like vim-plug, and for Tmux, you can use a tool like tpm (Tmux Plugin Manager). This way, you only need to specify the required plugins in your configuration files, and then run the corresponding commands to automatically install them.

item.description:
Machine Learning — Learning Theory

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Chapter 4

Part 6: Learning Theory

1 The bias/variance tradeoff

When we discussed linear regression, we considered the following question: when fitting the data, should we choose a “simple” model such as the linear model “$y = \theta_0 +\theta_1x$”, or a “complex” model such as the polynomial “$y= \theta_0 + \theta_1x+ ...+\theta_5x^5$”? This is illustrated below:

As the rightmost plot shows, fitting with a fifth-degree polynomial does not yield a good model. Moreover, although this fifth-degree polynomial gives a very good predicted value of $y$ (the corresponding housing price) for every $x$ in the training set (for example, the living area mentioned earlier in the notes), we still cannot expect this model to give reliable predictions for points outside the training set. In other words, a model obtained by learning from the training set with a high-degree polynomial of this kind simply does not carry over to other houses. The generalization error of a hypothesis (a formal definition will be given shortly) is precisely the expected error on examples that are not necessarily in the training set.

DTW was originally used to measure similarity between speech signals. The DTW algorithm is now commonly used to compute the similarity of two time series, especially series of different lengths and different rhythms.

Algorithm

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

ChatGPT evolved from InstructGPT.

Overview

Its training can be divided into four stages:

  1. Mask-based self-supervised training
  2. Supervised QA training on human-labeled data
  3. Supervised training on human rankings of answer preference
  4. Reinforcement learning from the learned human preferences to train a discriminative model

Self-supervised training

Self-supervised training is used for text generation. During training, the model is given the preceding words and asked to predict the next one. The prediction is a probability distribution over possible words, and beam search can sample the next word from it. That newly generated word is then fed back into the model to produce the following output. Because the output is obtained by random sampling, the result is different each time.

Suppose there is a vocabulary $\mathbf{V}=\{w_1,...,w_{|v|}\}$. For each word $w_i$, there are two ways to represent it: one-hot encoding, and distributed representation.

one-hot representation

Each word is represented as a vector whose length equals the total number of words in the vocabulary. Each vector has a single 1, and the remaining values are all 0.

Solving the Generalized Sylvester Equation

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Solving the Generalized Sylvester Equation

Common Sylvester Equations

The Sylvester equation

$$ \mathbf{AX}+\mathbf{XD} = \mathbf{E} $$

The generalized Sylvester equation

$$ \mathbf{AXB}+\mathbf{CXD} = \mathbf{E} $$

where $\mathbf{X}\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times r}$, $\mathbf{A}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $\mathbf{B}\in \mathbb{R}^{r\times p}$, $\mathbf{C}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, $\mathbf{D}\in \mathbb{R}^{r\times p}$, $\mathbf{E}\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times p}$.

The Stein matrix equation

$$ \mathbf{AXB}+\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{E} $$

The Lyapunov matrix equation

$$ \mathbf{AX}+\mathbf{XA^T}=\mathbf{E} $$
